content.comment_body: Hello everyone, I'm having trouble setting up multiple [product_name] modules to work with a single master for centralized start/stop control across all devices. In my trial project, I managed to connect three slaves before all network connections were used up. My setup involves an 80G ozone generator with the main module acting as the host. Using Q1, I activate both the air compressor and solenoid valve to push ozone gas out. The i1 input serves as the start/stop for both the host and all slave modules. I want to install several slave modules in different locations like rooms and pools—around six or more. The manual suggests support for up to 16 devices, but I can't figure out the configuration. Each slave, when activated by i1, should operate its local solenoid valve and also send the start/stop signal to the host, triggering the main compressor and valve. Is there a way to accomplish this using a single channel or marker that all devices send to the host? Any suggestions or examples would be appreciated.

I'm not entirely clear on your network setup between these modules. When creating your connections, you're using all 8 static connections for just 4 devices. Why do you have two connections between a master and a slave? Also, the concept of master/slave doesn't apply here as you've only added master modules in your network layout.

The main application works well with the ozone generator, and I have a demo video at [url]. In my test project, I didn't set up any network connections initially, but after adding Network Input/Output and configuring the IP, [product_name] software automatically creates two network connections per device. This quickly uses up all available connections. I even tried adding one slave to the project, but couldn't proceed with the schematic. My question is: what's the best way to use six or more modules, each with its own program, but ensure every unit can send start/stop commands to the main host? Could you provide a simple example project?

To clarify the basics of the master/slave configuration for these devices, no program can be stored on a slave unit—the slave only extends its hardware functionality to the master. Essentially, the slave acts as an expansion module for the master over Ethernet.

Here's an example: When using drag-and-drop to connect one diagram to another, always start with the same initial diagram. If you connect from device 1 to device 2, device 1 is the client and device 2 is the server, creating a client connection on device 1. Connecting back from device 2 to device 1 makes device 1 a server and device 2 a client, which adds another connection for both. This quickly uses up the available 8 static connections if you add several slaves.
I've attached your revised network project.

This was my goal, but I had a mistake in my network configuration. Connecting up to eight remote modules for control works perfectly and is sufficient for my needs. Thanks so much for your assistance!

analysis.insight_summary: The user faced challenges in setting up multiple [product_name] modules as distributed remote start/stop controls linked with a master device. Issues surfaced due to network connection limits in [product_name] configuration software and misunderstood master/slave roles. After guidance and corrections to the project setup, the user resolved the connection issues and successfully coordinated remote modules as intended.
analysis.user_expectations: The user wants simple configuration of numerous [product_name] modules in a centralized setup, using a shared start/stop signal across all devices, and efficient handling of network connections to allow scalable deployment.
pain_keywords: lack of guidance for master/slave setup
